subject: Math
cluster: A. Know number names and the count sequence.
text: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
ee_text: Starting with one, count to 10 by ones.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can count to 100 by ones, tens, and fives. I can count backwards from 100 by ones and tens. I can use my knowledge of counting to solve simple addition and subtraction problems. I can count objects in the real world and estimate their quantity. I can apply my counting skills to real-life situations, such as counting the number of steps to climb a staircase or the number of cookies on a plate.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can count to 100 by ones. I can skip count by 10s to 100. I can start counting at any number and count to 100.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can count to 50 by ones. I can skip count by 5s to 50. I can count forward from a random starting point to 100.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can count to 10 by ones. I can skip count by 2s to 10.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can starting with one, count to 10 by ones. I can Count number to 10 verbally. I can count without one-to-one correspondence to 10 starting with one by rote. I can sequentially sing numbers to 10 starting with one.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can count with teacher from one to two. I can count with the teacher to two.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can starting with one, count by ones to five. I can Count own fingers to five verbally. I can sequentially, count sequence to five either independent of objects, pictures, or things as a student would recite the alphabet or by pointing. I can Count without one-to-one correspondence to five. I can sequentially sing numbers to five. I can Sing along to counting song.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Know number names and the count sequence.
text: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.2.NBT.2c

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can count forward from a given number beyond the known sequence (e.g., starting at 15 and counting to 25). I can apply my counting skills to real-life situations, such as counting the number of steps I take to get to school or the number of cars that pass by my house in a minute. I can explain the strategies I use to count forward from a given number.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can consistently count forward from any given number within the known sequence (1-10, 1-20, etc.). I can use objects to help me count forward from a given number. I can explain how many objects I counted and how I got my answer.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can count forward from a given number within the known sequence, but I sometimes make mistakes or skip numbers. I can count forward from a given number within the known sequence, but I need help remembering the starting number.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can count forward from 1 to 10, but I need to start at 1 each time. I can count forward from a given number if it is within the first five numbers (1-5).
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.2.NBT.2c

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Know number names and the count sequence.
text: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.2.NBT.3

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can not only write numbers from 0 to 20, but I can also write them in different ways, such as using tally marks or Roman numerals. I can represent large numbers of objects (beyond 20) with written numerals. I can use my understanding of numbers to solve simple addition and subtraction problems in real-life situations. For example, I can figure out how many cookies are left after I eat some, or how many more toys I need to have the same amount as my friend.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can confidently write all numbers from 0 to 20. I can represent any number of objects (0-20) with a written numeral.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can write most numbers from 0 to 20 correctly. I can represent a number of objects (1-10) with a written numeral, but I may need help with larger numbers.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can write some numbers from 0 to 20, but I often forget or confuse them. I can sometimes represent a small number of objects (1-5) with a written numeral, but I struggle with larger numbers.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.2.NBT.3

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Tell the number of objects.
text: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality. a. When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object (one to one correspondence). Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted (cardinality). The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted (number conservation). c. Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger and the previous number is one smaller (hierarchical inclusion).
ee_text: Connect counting to cardinality to 10. a. Demonstrate one-to-one correspondence, pairing each object with one and only one number and each number with one and only one object (one-to-one correspondence). Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted (cardinality).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can count a large group of objects quickly and accurately. I can use my understanding of numbers to solve simple addition and subtraction problems. I can use my understanding of numbers to compare the quantities of different groups of objects. I can explain to someone else how to count objects and why it is important to count one-to-one.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can count objects in order, one-to-one, without skipping or repeating numbers. I understand that the last number I say tells me how many objects there are, and I can remember the number. I know that the number of objects is the same regardless of how they are arranged or the order in which I count them. I understand that each number name is one more than the previous number and one less than the next number.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can count objects in order, but sometimes I skip a number or say a number twice. I understand that the last number I say tells me how many objects there are, but I don't always remember the number. I can see that there are the same number of objects even if they are arranged differently.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can sometimes count objects, but I don't always say the number names in order. I sometimes forget to count all the objects or count some objects twice. I don't always understand that the last number I say tells me how many objects there are.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can starting with one, count to 10 by ones. I can count number to 10 verbally. I can count without one-to-one correspondence to 10 starting with one by rote. I can sequentially using numbers to 10 starting with one.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can count with teacher from one to two. I can count with the teacher to two.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can starting with one, count by ones to five. I can Count own fingers to five verbally. I can sequentially, count sequence to five either independent of objects, pictures, or things as a student would recite the alphabet or by pointing. I can count without one-to-one correspondence to five. I can sequentially using numbers to five. I can sing along to counting song.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Tell the number of objects.
text: Quickly recognize and name the quantity of up to 5 objects briefly shown in structured or unstructured arrangements without counting (perceptual subitizing).
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can quickly and consistently recognize and name the quantity of more than 5 objects shown briefly, regardless of their arrangement, without counting. I can use my subitizing skills to estimate the quantity of larger groups of objects quickly and efficiently. I can apply my subitizing skills to real-world situations, such as quickly determining the number of players on a sports team or the number of apples in a basket.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can quickly and consistently recognize the quantity of up to 5 objects shown briefly, regardless of their arrangement, without counting. I can quickly and consistently name the quantity of up to 5 objects shown briefly, regardless of their arrangement, without counting.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can consistently recognize the quantity of 3 or 4 objects shown briefly without counting. I can consistently name the quantity of 3 or 4 objects shown briefly without counting.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can sometimes recognize the quantity of 2 or 3 objects shown briefly without counting. I can sometimes name the quantity of 2 or 3 objects shown briefly without counting.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

subject: Math
cluster: B. Tell the number of objects.
text: Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1-20, count out that many objects.
ee_text: Count out up to three objects from a larger set, pairing each object with one and only one number name to tell how many.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can count large groups of objects efficiently by using strategies like skip counting or grouping. I can apply my counting skills to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how many cookies to bake for a party or how many people are in line at the store. I can explain my counting strategies and reasoning to others.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can count up to 20 objects arranged in a line, rectangular array, or circle. I can count out any number of objects from 1-20 when given the number. I can answer "how many?" questions for various arrangements of up to 20 objects.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can count up to 15 objects arranged in a line or rectangular array. I can count out 5-10 objects when given a number. I can answer "how many?" questions for simple arrangements of up to 10 objects.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can count up to 10 objects arranged in a line. I can identify the number of objects in a small group without counting individually.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can count out up to three objects from a larger set, pairing each object with one and only one number name to tell how many. For example, I can take three blocks from a pile and count them one by one, saying "one, two, three." I know that there are three blocks in total.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can start to count objects from a larger set, but I am still learning how to keep track of which objects I have counted. For example, I can take some marbles from a bag and try to count them, but I might lose track and count the same marble twice. I am still developing my understanding of one-to-one correspondence.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can count out up to three objects from a larger set, but I sometimes forget to say the number name for each object. For example, I can take three crayons from a box and count them, but I might only say "one, two" instead of "one, two, three." I am still learning to connect each object with a number name.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Compare Numbers
text: Identify whether the number of objects (up to 10) in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.
ee_text: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than (more) or less than (when the quantities are clearly different) or equal to the number objects in another group.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare the number of objects in two groups (up to 10) and solve word problems related to comparing quantities. I can use my understanding of comparing numbers to estimate the number of objects in a group without counting them all. I can create my own word problems that involve comparing the number of objects in two groups.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can identify whether a group of objects (up to 10) has more, less, or the same number of objects as another group by using matching and counting strategies. I can explain my reasoning by saying things like "There are 5 apples in this group and 3 apples in that group, so there are more apples in the first group."
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can match objects in two groups one-to-one and say which group has more or less based on whether I have any objects left over. I can count the objects in two groups and say which group has more or less based on the numbers.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify that there are more objects in a group when it has more objects than I can count on my fingers. I can tell which group has fewer objects by looking at the groups and saying which one has "less."
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can look at two groups of objects and tell you which group has more, less, or the same number of objects. I can use words like "more," "less," and "equal" to describe the number of objects in different groups. I can compare the number of objects in two groups by counting the objects in each group and comparing the numbers. I can use objects to represent the numbers in two groups and compare the quantities.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I am starting to understand the concepts of "more" and "less." I can sometimes identify which group has more objects when the difference is very obvious. I am beginning to use objects to represent numbers. I need support to compare the number of objects in two groups.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can sometimes identify which group has more or less objects, especially when the difference is large. I can use the words "more" and "less" to describe the number of objects in different groups. I can start to compare the number of objects in two groups by counting the objects in each group. I can use objects to represent the numbers in two groups, but I may need help comparing the quantities.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Compare Numbers
text: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals using student generated ways to record the comparison.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.4 and M.EE.2.NBT.4.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare two numbers between 1 and 10 and explain the difference between them. I can apply my understanding of number comparison to solve real-world problems. I can create my own methods for comparing numbers, such as using place value or mental math strategies. I can explain my methods to others and justify my reasoning.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can accurately compare any two numbers between 1 and 10, regardless of their order. I can explain my reasoning using clear and precise language. I can record the comparison using symbols (>, <, =) and student-generated methods (number lines, drawings, manipulatives).
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can correctly identify the larger number when comparing two single-digit numbers. I can use manipulatives or drawings to represent the two numbers and compare them. I can use informal language and symbols (>, <) to record the comparison.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify the two numbers being compared. I can attempt to compare the two numbers using informal language ("bigger," "smaller").
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.4 and M.EE.2.NBT.4.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand addition as putting together and adding to and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
text: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, or numbers. Drawings need not show details but should show the mathematics in the problem.
ee_text: Represent addition as “putting together” or subtraction as “taking from” in everyday activities (e.g., with objects, fingers, sounds, drawings, verbal explanations, or numbers).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use manipulatives to solve addition and subtraction problems beyond 10. I can write number sentences to represent addition and subtraction problems. I can apply my understanding of addition and subtraction to real-world situations, such as combining groups of objects or figuring out how many objects are left after sharing. I can explain my reasoning and strategies for solving addition and subtraction problems.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can represent addition and subtraction using objects, fingers, drawings, and numbers within 10. I can explain my thinking when solving addition and subtraction problems. I can create drawings that accurately represent the addition or subtraction problem.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can use objects to demonstrate adding and subtracting within 5. I can draw simple pictures to represent adding and subtracting within 5. I can explain, in my own words, what happens when we add or subtract objects.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can clap my hands to represent adding two objects together. I can hold up my fingers to represent taking away one object from a group.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can represent addition as “putting together” or subtraction as “taking from” in everyday activities. I can identify the total number of crayons when one student has three crayons and another student has two, and they put their crayons together to share. Describe the action as put together. I can add to a group of crayons when told to add to group. I can take away from a group of crayons when told to take away from the group. I can given five stickers, give another student one of the five stickers, and describes the action as take away. I can join linking cubes to show action/process of putting together or addition. I can break apart linking cubes/snap blocks/bristle blocks/pop-beads to show action/process of taking from or subtraction.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can put together” or “take from” with teacher. I can together with a teacher add a block to a stack while teacher says, “put together.” I can together with a teacher take a block from a stack while the teacher says, “take away.”
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can follow directions to “put together” by adding one or “take from” by taking one. I can, if given a bowl of counting bears, add a counting bear to the bowl. The teacher calls the action “putting together” or addition. I can take one when the teacher is passing out supplies and directs the students to take one. The teacher calls the action “taking away” or subtraction. I can place popsicle sticks into a circle and use language to describe addition or “putting together”. I can, using cubes, create towers by adding or taking away one cube at a time. I can remove popsicle sticks from a circle and use language to describe subtraction or “taking from”.

cluster: A. Understand addition as putting together and adding to and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can solve addition and subtraction word problems involving numbers up to 10. I can use objects, drawings, and number sentences to represent addition and subtraction problems. I can explain my thinking when solving addition and subtraction problems. I can use different strategies to solve addition and subtraction problems.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can solve simple addition and subtraction word problems involving numbers up to 5. I can use objects or drawings to represent addition and subtraction problems. I can explain my thinking when solving addition and subtraction problems.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand addition as putting together and adding to and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
text: Compose and decompose quantities within 10. a. Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition with drawings or numbers. Quickly name the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements anchored to 5 (e.g., fingers, ten frames, math rack/rekenrek) with totals up to 10 without counting by recognizing the arrangement or seeing the quantity in subgroups that are combined (conceptual subitizing).
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.6.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can decompose any number less than or equal to 10 into pairs in multiple ways using objects, drawings, or mental math and explain my reasoning. I can instantly recognize the quantity of objects briefly shown in various arrangements, even those not anchored to 5, with totals beyond 10. I can apply my understanding of composing and decomposing quantities to solve real-world problems, such as figuring out how many pieces of fruit I need to buy to make a fruit salad for a certain number of people.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can decompose any number less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way using objects or drawings and record each decomposition with drawings or numbers. I can quickly name the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements anchored to 5 (e.g., fingers, ten frames, math rack/rekenrek) with totals up to 10 without counting by recognizing the arrangement or seeing the quantity in subgroups that are combined.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can decompose most numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs using objects or drawings. I can often recognize the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements up to 10 without counting. I can sometimes decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into subgroups that are combined.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can decompose some numbers less than or equal to 5 into pairs using objects or drawings. I can sometimes recognize the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements up to 5 without counting.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.6.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand addition as putting together and adding to and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
text: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or numbers.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.2.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use objects or drawings to find the missing number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9. I can explain my thinking using words or pictures. I can apply this skill to real-life situations. For example, I can use my fingers to figure out how many more cookies I need to eat to have 10 total.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use objects or drawings to find the missing number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9. I can record the answer with a drawing or numbers. For example, if I see 3 objects, I can draw 7 more objects to show that 3 + 7 = 10.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify all numbers from 1 to 9. I can count objects up to 10. I can use objects to show that 5 + 5 = 10.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify some numbers from 1 to 9. I can count objects up to 5.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.2.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand addition as putting together and adding to and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
text: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 5 using mental images and composing/decomposing numbers up to 5.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.4 and M.EE.1.NBT.6.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can add and subtract within 5 fluently and automatically. I can apply my understanding of addition and subtraction to solve real-world problems. subject: Math
strand: Number and Operations in Base Ten
cluster: A. Work with numbers 11- 19 to gain foundations for place value.
text: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or numbers; understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.1.NBT.4 and M.EE.1.NBT.6.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use objects, drawings, or numbers to show that 12 is made up of 10 and 2. I can also explain how this helps me understand other math concepts, such as place value and addition. subject: Math
cluster: A. Describe and compare measurable attributes.
text: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.
ee_text: Classify objects according to attributes (e.g., big/small, heavy/light).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can: Describe several measurable attributes of a single object and use this information to solve real-world problems. Example: A student wants to wrap a gift box that is 12 inches long, 8 inches wide, and 5 inches tall. They measure the wrapping paper and determine they need a piece that is at least 30 inches long and 20 inches wide to cover the box completely. They also calculate the amount of ribbon needed to tie a bow around the box based on its circumference.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can: Describe several measurable attributes of a single object, using appropriate vocabulary for length, weight, capacity, and other measurable features. Example: A student picks up a book and says, "This book is about 10 inches long, 8 inches wide, and 2 inches thick. It weighs about 2 pounds and has 200 pages."
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can: Identify two measurable attributes of an object, such as its size and color. Example: A student holds up a small blue cube and says, "It's small and blue."
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can: Identify one measurable attribute of an object, such as its color or shape. Example: A student points to a red ball and says, "It's red!"
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can classify objects according to attributes (big/small, heavy/light). I can, if given a big book and a small book, describe or demonstrate which one is bigger and which one is smaller. I can, if given the shoe of a student and the teacher, identify which one is bigger and which one is smaller. I can, sort heavy and light objects according to weight. I can, if given the hand of a student in the class and the hand of the teacher, identify which one is bigger and which one is smaller. I can, if given two objects of varying weight, describe or demonstrate which is heavy/light or large/small.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can match objects by attribute big and small. I can touch a large object (such as a pumpkin) as teacher describes it as big when compared to a smaller pumpkin toy. I can indicate small pumpkin as teacher describes it as small when compared with a large pumpkin. I can indicate if I want the big ball or the small ball.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can use a model or a template, sort objects by one attribute (big/small or heavy/light). I can sort counting bears by size using a model or template. I can, if given two objects, where one is at least twice the size of the other, identify which one is bigger and which one is smaller with descriptive prompts from the teacher. I can identify bigger ball when shown a beach ball and a tennis ball, and listening to the teacher use voice inflections and kinesthetic motions to exaggerate bigger and smaller. I can identify the bigger ball when shown a golf ball and beach ball and listening to the teacher using voice inflections and motions to exaggerate. I can Sort objects in the classroom into groups of heavy and light (e.g., bowling ball, beach ball, and a rock). I can, if given two pictures of real-life objects, select the bigger one.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
text: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has "more of" / "less of" the attribute and describe the difference. * For example, directly compare the heights of two children and describe one child as taller/shorter.
ee_text: Classify objects according to attributes (e.g., big/small, heavy/light).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute and explain the real-world implications of the difference. I can use multiple units of measurement to compare the objects, converting between units as needed. I can create a visual representation of the comparison, such as a graph or chart. I can use my understanding of measurement and comparison to solve real-world problems, such as determining how much fabric is needed to make a dress or how much water to fill a pool.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute and describe one object as having "more of" or "less of" the attribute. I can use standard units of measurement to quantify the difference between the objects, such as inches or centimeters. I can use precise language to describe the difference, such as "5 inches taller" or "2 centimeters shorter." I can explain my reasoning for choosing the object with more or less of the attribute.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can compare two objects with a measurable attribute and state which object has more or less of the attribute. I can use comparative language to describe the difference, such as "longer" or "shorter." I can use non-standard units of measurement to compare the objects, such as hand spans or footsteps.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify that two objects have a measurable attribute in common, such as color or size. I can use basic vocabulary to describe the attribute, such as "big" or "small."

Then, when shown two objects that match the previously presented objects, place them with the matching object to make a group (two cubes, two pyramids). I can Group objects into like sets.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can separate objects into two groups. I can when given an assortment of objects, divide into two groups and indicate how many in each group. I can when given counting cubes in two sizes, sort them into two piles.

descriptors.ee_emerging: I can identify which group has more or less when objects are added or taken away. I can answer a question like: when an object is added to a group of three, “Is this more?” and “Is this less?” I can answer a question like: when an object is taken from a group of three, “Is this more?” and “Is this less?”
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can use addition to find the total number of objects. I can Three apples + four apples = six apples. I can add to find the total number of stars. I can Skip count by twos to tell how many.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Represent and solve problems involving multiplica- tion and division.
text: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem. See Appendix, Tables 2A and 2B for specific problem situations.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.3.OA.1 and M.EE.5.NBT.5.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve word problems involving multiplication and division within 100 using different strategies like drawings or equations (e.g., "I solved a problem using arrays and found that 4 x 8 = 32"). I can create my own word problems that involve equal groups or arrays and explain my solution.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use multiplication or division to solve word problems with equal groups (e.g., "I used multiplication to find the total items in 5 groups of 6"). I can use equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can start to solve word problems with equal groups by using repeated addition or subtraction, with help (e.g., "With guidance, I used repeated addition to solve 3 groups of 7"). I can draw arrays to help me understand multiplication and division problems.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can use objects or drawings to solve simple word problems involving groups, with help (e.g., "With support, I used counters to find how many are in 4 groups of 3"). I can start to recognize word problems involving equal groups, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.3.OA.1 and M.EE.5.NBT.5.

subject: Math
cluster: B. Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.
text: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide. Student use of the formal terms for these properties is not necessary. Examples: If 6 x 4 = 24 is known, then 4 x 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 x 5 x 2 can be found by 3 x 5 = 15, then 15 x 2 = 30, or by 5 x 2 = 10, then 3 x 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 x 5 = 40 and 8 x 2 = 16, one can find 8 x 7 as 8 x (5 + 2) = (8 x 5) + (8 x 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE. N.CN.2.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use properties like the commutative and associative properties of multiplication to solve problems (e.g., "I know 4 x 6 = 6 x 4, and I use that to solve multiplication faster"). I can explain how I applied a property of multiplication or division to find the answer to a problem.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use properties of multiplication to help me multiply or divide in different ways (e.g., "I used the distributive property to solve 8 x 7 by breaking it into 8 x (5 + 2)"). I can find the answer to a multiplication or division problem by rearranging the factors.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can start to use properties like switching the order of numbers to help me multiply or divide, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I switched 3 x 4 to 4 x 3 and got the same answer"). I can try breaking down numbers in multiplication with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can start to understand that I can add groups in any order to find the same answer, with help (e.g., "With support, I know that 2 x 5 and 5 x 2 both equal 10"). I can use basic addition to understand multiplication with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE. N.CN.2.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.
text: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem. * For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve division problems by thinking of them as unknown-factor problems (e.g., "I solved 32 ÷ 8 by asking, 'What number times 8 equals 32?'"). I can explain my thinking when solving division problems using multiplication relationships.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use multiplication to solve division problems by finding the missing factor (e.g., "I figured out 24 ÷ 4 by knowing that 4 x 6 = 24"). I can understand that division and multiplication are related and use this to solve problems.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can try using multiplication to help solve simple division problems, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I used 3 x 5 = 15 to understand 15 ÷ 3"). I can recognize that division can be solved by finding a missing number with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to understand that division involves finding a missing factor, with help (e.g., "With support, I figured out that 12 ÷ 3 needs the number that makes 12 when multiplied by 3"). I can use multiplication facts to try solving division with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

subject: Math
cluster: C. Multiply and divide within 100.
text: Use multiplicative thinking to multiply and divide within 100. a. Use the meanings of multiplication and division, the relationship between the operations (e.g., knowing that 8 x 5 = 40, one could reason that 40 ÷ 5 = 8), and properties of operations (e.g., the distributive property) to develop and understand strategies to multiply and divide within 100. * Flexibly and efficiently use strategies, the relationship between the operations, and properties of operations to find products and quotients with multiples of 0, 1, 2, 5, & 10 within 100.
ee_text: Solve addition and subtraction problems within 20, when the result is unknown.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use multiplication and division strategies flexibly to find answers quickly within 100 (e.g., "I used the distributive property to solve 8 x 7 as (8 x 5) + (8 x 2) = 40 + 16 = 56"). I can explain how multiplication and division are related and use that relationship to check my answers.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use multiplication and division strategies within 100, like skip counting and arrays, to find answers accurately (e.g., "I used an array to solve 6 x 8 = 48"). I can use my knowledge of multiplication to solve division problems within 100 and check my answers.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can solve multiplication and division problems with numbers within 100 by using basic strategies like repeated addition or subtraction, with guidance (e.g., "With help, I used repeated addition to find 5 x 6"). I can start using multiplication facts to solve division problems within 100 with some support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can solve simple multiplication or division problems with numbers within 10 by using objects or drawings, with help (e.g., "With support, I used counters to solve 4 x 3"). I can start to see how multiplication and division are related with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can solve addition and subtraction problems with numbers up to 20 to find the answer. I can add or subtract numbers within 20 to figure out the total or what’s left when one part is missing.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can use objects to show adding or taking away up to 5 items with support. I can find the total or what’s left with hands-on help, using numbers up to 5.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can solve simple addition or subtraction problems within 10 to find the answer with help. I can use objects or fingers to add or take away items and find the result within 10 with guidance.

subject: Math
cluster: D. Solve problems involving the four operations and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.
text: Solve two-step word problems, posed with whole numbers and having whole number answers, using the four operations. Represent these problems using one or two equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. If one equation is used, grouping symbols (i.e., parentheses) may be needed. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.
ee_text: Solve one-step real-world problems within 20, using addition or subtraction.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve two-step word problems using all four operations and explain my solution using equations with grouping symbols (e.g., "I solved (3 + 2) x 4 = 20 to find the answer and explained why I used parentheses"). I can check my answer by estimating and using mental math to decide if it is reasonable.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can solve two-step word problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division and write an equation to represent the problem with a letter for the unknown (e.g., "I used 3 + 2 x 4 = 20 and labeled the unknown as 'x'"). I can estimate my answer to decide if it makes sense.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can solve simple two-step word problems with some guidance and write a basic equation using an unknown letter (e.g., "With help, I used 10 - 3 + 5 = 12 and labeled the unknown as 'x'"). I can try using mental math to check if my answer is reasonable, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin solving basic two-step word problems by adding and subtracting numbers with help (e.g., "With support, I solved 5 + 3 - 2 for a simple word problem"). I can start to use mental math or simple estimation to check if my answer is close, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can solve real-world problems by adding or subtracting numbers up to 20 to find the answer. I can use addition or subtraction to figure out real-life situations, like finding out how many are left or the total when combining items.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can use objects to add or take away items in a real-world situation with numbers up to 5 with support. I can understand and solve simple problems about adding or subtracting small numbers with help.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can solve simple addition or subtraction problems within 10 about real-life situations with help. I can use objects or pictures to add or subtract in real-world situations with numbers up to 10 with guidance.

subject: Math
cluster: D. Solve problems involving the four operations and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.
text: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table) and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.
ee_text: Identify arithmetic patterns.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can find and explain patterns in the multiplication table, like how multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5, and use properties of operations to explain why the pattern works. I can describe how properties like the distributive property help explain patterns I see in both addition and multiplication tables.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can identify patterns in addition and multiplication tables, like how multiples of 2 are always even, and explain them using properties of operations (e.g., "I know 4 times any number is even because 4 can be split into two equal groups"). I can describe arithmetic patterns and use terms like “commutative property” to explain why they happen.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find simple patterns in the addition and multiplication tables, like counting by 2s or 5s, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I see that 3 x 4 is the same as 4 x 3"). I can try to explain why some patterns occur by using addition or multiplication examples, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can start to recognize basic patterns in addition and multiplication tables, like seeing that even numbers in the table repeat, with help (e.g., "With support, I noticed that all numbers in the 2’s row are even"). I can use simple examples to begin to understand patterns, like seeing how adding the same number makes a sequence, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can add to solve real world one-step story problems from 0-30. Represent the problem in pictures or with objects. I can solve by adding (e.g., “Here are 10 pencils. We need 10 more for each person to get a pencil. How many will we need in all?”) I can solve by adding (e.g., “Connie had five marbles. Juan gave her eight more marbles. How many marbles does Connie have all together?”) I can solve by adding (e.g., “Add the crayons in these two boxes and show me how many we have in all.”)
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can identify the object(s) that appear in a real world one-step story problem. I can when given a simple word problem and asked “What is the problem about?” point to an object from a choice of two that represents what the problem was about (e.g., box, toy). I can Indicate which object a word problem is about from an array of two choices.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can add to solve word problems identified through symbol representation. I can complete word problems that have pictures rather than words. I can solve by adding (e.g., “There are three ducks in the pond, two more joined. How many ducks are in the pond?” [picture representation])

subject: Math
strand: Number and Operations in Base Ten
cluster: A. Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic, using a variety of strategies.
text: Use place value understanding to generate estimates for problems in real-world situations, with whole numbers within 1,000, using strategies such as mental math, benchmark numbers, compatible numbers, and rounding. Assess the reasonableness of their estimates (e.g., Is my estimate too low or too high? What degree of precision do I need for this situation?).
ee_text: Use decade numbers (10, 20, 30) as benchmarks to demonstrate understanding of place value for numbers 0-30.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use place value to round and estimate answers for problems within 1,000, explaining if my answer is reasonable (e.g., "I rounded 756 to 800 and knew my estimate was close to the real answer"). I can choose the best level of precision for an estimate based on the problem context.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use place value to estimate answers by rounding numbers within 1,000 (e.g., "I rounded 342 to 340 to estimate a total quickly"). I can explain if my estimate is too high or too low and adjust if needed.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can estimate answers by rounding to the nearest ten or hundred with some help (e.g., "With guidance, I rounded 590 to 600"). I can use place value to make simple guesses about sums or differences.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can start to understand that rounding helps make estimates faster, with support (e.g., "With help, I rounded 130 to 100 to make estimating easier"). I can try using place value to compare numbers and make estimates with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can identify the two 10s a number comes in between on a number line (numbers 0-30). I can use a color-beaded number line to identify the two 10s a number falls between. I can when given the number 14, identify 10 and 20.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can identify a number. I can point to any number from one to three on a number line. I can participate in a cakewalk. when the music stops, look to see if they are on the number that is called out. I can identify a number when point to or presented on a card. I can when given a number from one to three, point to the number symbol.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can identify tens on a number line. I can when given a number line, circle the tens. I can stand on a number chart on 10, 20, 30, etc.

subject: Math
strand: Number and Operations in Base Ten
cluster: A. Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic, using a variety of strategies.
text: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 1,000 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
ee_text: Demonstrate understanding of place value to tens.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use place value strategies and properties of addition and subtraction to quickly solve problems within 1,000 (e.g., "I solved 630 + 290 by breaking it down to 600 + 300 and adding the tens separately"). I can explain my thinking when adding or subtracting large numbers and check my answers for accuracy.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can add and subtract numbers within 1,000 by using place value to make the calculation easier (e.g., "I used place value to add 250 + 450 as 200 + 400 and 50 + 50"). I can use strategies like regrouping to add or subtract accurately within 1,000.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can add and subtract numbers within 1,000 using place value, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I broke 430 into hundreds and tens to add it to 260"). I can try using the relationship between addition and subtraction to solve problems with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin adding and subtracting numbers within 100 using place value strategies, with help (e.g., "With support, I added 80 + 20 by thinking of it as 8 tens plus 2 tens"). I can start to understand that place value helps with adding and subtracting larger numbers with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can identify place value to tens. I can when given two-digit number cards, identify the number in the tens place value. I can when given a group of 10 frame models, arrange and count the value of the number. I can answer a question like: I saw three groups of 10 and five extras, so three groups of 10 = 30 and 5 more makes 35.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can identify more or less. I can identify given two collections of objects (group of 10, group of 20), indicate, “Which has more?” I can when given math manipulatives representing a single unit and multiple units, point to the multiple unit representation when asked “which is more?”
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can count to 10 using one-to-one correspondence. I can when given a bag of Skittles, pull 10 Skittles out of the bag. I can select a domino and tell what number the dots represent. I can Shown a set of 10 objects, create a duplicate collection. I can when given a container of pennies, count out 10 from the container.

subject: Math
strand: Number and Operations in Base Ten
cluster: A. Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic, using a variety of strategies.
text: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (e.g., 9 x 80, 5 x 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations. * Grade 3 assessment expectations for Mathematics in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8, but students should also have instructional experiences with other sized fractions.
ee_text: Count by tens using models (e.g., objects, base ten blocks, money).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can multiply one-digit numbers by multiples of 10 using place value to make quick calculations (e.g., "I solved 4 x 50 by thinking of 4 times 5 tens as 20 tens, which is 200"). I can explain my strategy for multiplying by multiples of 10 and check my answer for accuracy.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 using place value (e.g., "I solved 6 x 30 by thinking of it as 6 times 3 tens, which is 180"). I can use my understanding of place value to multiply accurately within 90.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 with some help (e.g., "With guidance, I solved 3 x 20 by counting three groups of 20"). I can try using place value to understand multiplication with multiples of 10.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to multiply small numbers by 10 using objects or repeated addition with help (e.g., "With support, I used repeated addition to find 2 x 10 as 10 + 10 = 20"). I can start to understand that multiplying by 10 means adding groups of 10 with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can count by tens using money. I can when given three dimes, count by 10 to determine total. I can when given five dimes, count by 10 to determine total.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can count objects to 10.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can identify whole numbers to 10. I can when given sets of 10 pennies, pair with numbers. I can when given sets of 10 pennies, pair with dimes.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.
text: Understand a unit fraction as the quantity formed when a whole is partitioned into equal parts and explain that a unit fraction is one of those parts (e.g., 1/4). Understand fractions are composed of unit fractions. For example, 7/4 is the quantity formed by 7 parts of the size 1/4.
ee_text: Differentiate a fractional part from a whole.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain that unit fractions show one part of a whole divided into equal parts and use them to make larger fractions (e.g., "I know that 3/4 is made of three 1/4 parts"). I can describe how unit fractions combine to make other fractions, like 5/8.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can identify a unit fraction as one part of a whole divided into equal parts (e.g., "I know that 1/3 means one part of something divided into three equal parts"). I can use models like fraction circles or number lines to show unit fractions.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify a unit fraction on a number line or in a shape, with some help (e.g., "With help, I found 1/4 as one of four equal parts"). I can understand that fractions represent equal parts of a whole with guidance.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can start to recognize unit fractions, like 1/2 and 1/4, as parts of a whole with support (e.g., "With help, I know that 1/2 means one part of a whole split in half"). I can use simple shapes like circles or rectangles to see how they can be divided into equal parts, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can understand 2/4 = 1/2. I can when given two rectangles, cut one rectangle into half and a second into fourths and compare the rectangles to determine how many fourths equal a half. I can work with two rectangles of the same size, fold one rectangle in half and the other in fourths and compare to find how many fourths equal half. I can use a picture of two circles, cut one in half and the other in fourths and compare them to find how many fourths equal half.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can understand that two halves is equivalent to one whole. I can wooden shapes are separated into halves and put back together into a whole. I can Plastic eggs are broken into halves and put back to whole.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can understand 4/4 or 2/2 = 1. I can Complete two- and four-piece puzzles. I can play a game with self-sticking non-adhesive pieces that make a whole.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.
text: Understand and represent a fraction as a number on the number line. a. Understand the whole on a number line is defined as the interval from 0 to 1 and the unit fraction is defined by partitioning the interval into equal parts (i.e., equal-sized lengths).
ee_text: M.EE.3.NF.2 Differentiate a fractional part from a whole.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can represent fractions on a number line, explaining how each part represents a unit fraction and how this builds from 0 to 1 (e.g., "I showed that 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and 4/4 build from 0 to 1 on a number line"). I can use number lines to compare and order fractions, explaining how each fraction’s location represents its size.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can place unit fractions and fractions like 1/2 or 3/4 on a number line, showing how they fit between 0 and 1 (e.g., "I placed 1/3 on the number line by dividing the interval from 0 to 1 into three equal parts"). I can explain that fractions are numbers and that the number line can represent their size from 0 to 1.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify and place simple fractions like 1/2 on a number line with some help (e.g., "With guidance, I placed 1/2 between 0 and 1 on a number line"). I can start to understand that the space between 0 and 1 on a number line can be divided into equal parts.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to see that fractions can be placed on a number line, with support (e.g., "With help, I placed 1/2 on a line between 0 and 1"). I can try using a number line to see where fractions fit between whole numbers with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can tell the difference between a whole object and a part of an object, like knowing that one piece is a part of a whole pizza. I can identify when something is divided into parts and recognize one part as a fraction of the whole.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can look at two objects and show which one is whole and which one is a part with support. I can point to a part of an object and understand it is not the whole with help.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can point to a whole object and a part of that object when asked, with help. I can recognize a piece or part of something, like a slice of an apple, as part of the whole object with guidance.

source: CCEE Math Standards 2024 V1 Complete.xlsx (school)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.
text: Represent fractions on a number line by iterating lengths of the unit fraction from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval represents the size of the fraction and that its endpoint locates the fraction as a number on the number line. * For example, 5/3 indicates the length of a line segment from 0 by iterating the unit fraction 1/3 five times and its end point locates the fraction 5/3 on the number line.
ee_text: Not Applicable

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can represent fractions greater than 1 by iterating unit fractions beyond the interval from 0 to 1 (e.g., "I showed 5/3 by counting five 1/3 units from 0 on the number line"). I can explain how each step on the number line corresponds to one unit fraction, and use this to locate fractions like 7/4 and 8/3.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can represent fractions by marking each unit fraction on a number line, showing where they end between 0 and 1 (e.g., "I placed 3/4 by moving three 1/4 lengths from 0"). I can explain that each step from 0 to a fraction is a repeated unit fraction that shows its size.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can place simple fractions on a number line by counting unit fractions with some help (e.g., "With guidance, I marked 1/3, 2/3, and 3/3 on a number line"). I can try using repeated parts to place fractions between 0 and 1 on a number line, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to understand that fractions can be placed by repeating equal parts on a number line, with support (e.g., "With help, I marked 1/4 and 2/4 on a line from 0 to 1"). I can try using simple steps on a number line to see how fractions build up from 0, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not Applicable

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.
text: Explain equivalence of fractions and compare fractions by reasoning about their size. a. Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size or name the same point on a number line.
ee_text: M.EE.3.NF.3 Differentiate a fractional part from a whole.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain why some fractions are equivalent using visual models and describe the relationship (e.g., "I know that 1/2 is the same as 2/4 because two 1/4 pieces equal one 1/2"). I can compare fractions with different numerators and denominators by using models and explain which is larger or smaller.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can recognize equivalent fractions like 1/2 and 2/4 by comparing their size using visual models (e.g., "I know that 1/2 and 2/4 are the same size when I look at a model"). I can compare two fractions with the same numerator or denominator and explain which one is larger or smaller.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can start to identify some simple equivalent fractions using models, with help (e.g., "With guidance, I can see that 1/2 and 2/4 cover the same area on a fraction bar"). I can compare fractions with the same denominator by looking at which has more parts, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to understand that fractions like 1/2 and 2/4 can represent the same amount, with support (e.g., "With help, I know that 1/2 is like 2 out of 4 equal parts"). I can start to compare fractions with the same denominator by looking at visual models, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can differentiate between whole, half, and fourth. I can use fraction strips and fraction tiles to identify whole and half, and which is more. I can use squares of paper, fold it in 1/2 and 1/4 and identify the parts.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can recognize that fractions are part of a whole. I can use a self-sticking non-adhesive shape, take apart and put together fractional parts of a whole. I can utilize wooden shapes, separate into halves and put back together into whole. I can when shown pictures of the whole class and part of the class, select the picture that shows part of the class upon request.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can differentiate between whole and half. I can when given a whole sandwich versus a half sandwich cut horizontally, vertically, and diagonally select the whole or half upon request. I can show the halfway point on a number line. I can with pictures cut into halves and pictures not cut, sort the pictures into halves and wholes.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.
text: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3) and explain why the fractions are equivalent by using a visual fraction model (e.g., tape diagram or number line).

descriptors.cc_approaching: I can recognize simple equivalent fractions, with some guidance, and start using visual models to show them (e.g., "With help, I showed that 1/2 equals 2/4 on a fraction bar"). subject: Math
cluster: A. Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.

ee_text: Tell time to the hour on a digital clock.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can tell and write time to the nearest minute and solve word problems that involve adding or subtracting minutes (e.g., "I figured out that 15 minutes after 3:10 is 3:25"). I can explain my strategy for finding elapsed time in word problems and check my answers for accuracy.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can tell and write time to the nearest minute on analog and digital clocks (e.g., "I read 3:27 on the clock and wrote it down"). I can solve simple word problems that ask me to add or subtract time intervals.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can tell time to the nearest 5 minutes and start to add or subtract time intervals, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I figured out that 10 minutes after 2:30 is 2:40"). I can begin writing time to the nearest minute on digital clocks with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can read time to the nearest 5 minutes on an analog or digital clock with support (e.g., "With help, I know it’s 3:10 when the minute hand is on the 2"). I can start to understand that time intervals show how long things take, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can tell time to the hour on a digital clock. I can when given a time written to the hour, write the digital time. I can identify the time of a digital clock that is set to the hour. I can when given a time on a digital clock, say the time to the hour.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can differentiate a digital clock from other measurement tools as a tool for telling time. I can when given a digital clock and a measuring cup, identify the clock for telling time. I can when asked, “How do we know when it is time to go to lunch?” indicate a clock.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can identify which is the hour on a digital clock. I can Relate the hour with the time on their daily schedule. I can when given cards showing digital clocks - with one clock having the hour circled and one clock with the minutes circled, indicate the clock with the hour circled.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.
text: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l), excluding compound units such as cm3 and finding the geometric volume of a container. ee_text: Identify the appropriate measurement tool to solve one- step word problems involving mass and volume.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can measure and estimate volumes and masses in grams, kilograms, and liters and solve real-world problems using these measurements (e.g., "I used a beaker to measure 500 ml of water and estimated that’s about half of a liter"). descriptors.cc_at_target: I can measure volumes in liters and masses in grams or kilograms using standard tools (e.g., "I measured the weight of an apple as 100 grams"). I can use measurement data to solve one-step word problems involving volume or mass.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can measure and estimate liquid volumes or masses with some guidance and recognize the units (e.g., "With help, I measured a bottle with 200 ml of water"). I can solve simple word problems with volume or mass using tools like scales or measuring cups, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to understand that volume is measured in liters and mass is measured in grams or kilograms, with support (e.g., "With help, I know a liter is used to measure liquids"). I can use simple tools like a measuring cup to estimate small amounts of liquid with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can identify standard units of measure for mass and liquid. I can sort the following real-world items as being measured by grams or liters when shown the measurement tools (apple measured in grams and juice in liters). I can when shown pictures of the tool, identify what would be measured grams or liters.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can determine if an object is a solid and a liquid. I can place objects from the room into the appropriate measurement category (solid or liquid). I can when given a rock and a glass of water, identify which is solid.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can select the appropriate tool to measure a solid or a liquid. I can when provided two pictures, one showing a ruler and one showing a scale, identify which tool measures mass. I can when provided two tools, a measuring cup and a scale, identify which tool measures liquid. I can select from a variety of tools the appropriate tool to measure either mass or volume. I can when given a rock and a glass of water, identify which would be measured using a measuring cup.

subject: Math

descriptors.cc_at_target: I can draw a scaled picture or bar graph and use it to answer questions about the data (e.g., "I drew a bar graph with each bar representing 2 votes and answered questions about the most popular choice"). descriptors.cc_approaching: I can draw a simple bar or picture graph with some guidance, and answer questions about the data (e.g., "With help, I drew a picture graph and counted each picture to answer questions"). I can compare amounts in different categories by looking at my graph with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to understand that bar and picture graphs represent data in categories, with support (e.g., "With help, I know that each picture represents a number of things"). I can try using a graph to answer simple questions with guidance.

descriptors.ee_approaching: I can organize data. I can take data collected from the lunch choices and place data into appropriate categories. I can place data on a chart to represent the data collected.

subject: Math
cluster: B. Represent and interpret data.
text: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units -- whole numbers, halves, fourths.
ee_text: Measure the length of objects using standard tools including rulers, yardsticks, and meter sticks.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can measure lengths to the nearest 1/4 inch and use my measurements to create a line plot with appropriate scales (e.g., "I measured objects to the nearest 1/4 inch and created a line plot to show the results"). I can analyze my line plot to answer questions and describe patterns in the data.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can measure lengths to the nearest 1/2 or 1/4 inch and use my measurements to make a line plot (e.g., "I used a ruler to measure items to the nearest 1/4 inch and plotted them on a line"). I can answer questions about the data in my line plot, like finding the longest or shortest measurement.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can measure lengths to the nearest 1/2 inch and record my measurements on a line plot, with guidance (e.g., "With help, I measured objects to the nearest 1/2 inch and added them to a line plot"). I can compare measurements on the line plot, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to measure lengths to the nearest inch and place my measurements on a line plot, with support (e.g., "With help, I measured items to the nearest inch and put the measurements on a line plot"). I can start to understand that a line plot shows measurements in order, with guidance.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can measure length of objects using standard tools, such as rulers, yardsticks, and meter sticks. I can when given an object and a measuring tool, use the tool to mark the length of the object. I can when given a ruler and snowfall, mark the depth of the snow with a ruler. I can when given a yardstick, measure different lengths or widths of the room and record the measurement.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can place a standard measuring tool where one would begin to measure the length of an object. I can when given a string, place the ruler at the end of the string where one would begin a measure. I can Shown a picture of a boy standing against a height measure, and asked where you would look to find the boy’s height, indicate the top of the boy’s head. I can when given a bookshelf and a ruler, place the ruler on the lower left corner of the bookshelf front. (Anything with a definite lower left edge that will not allow the student to go beyond it will work.)
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can Measure length with non-standard units of measurement. I can identify the length of items in the classroom using a yardstick end-to- end and record as number of yardsticks. I can when provided two non-standard measuring units, identify which one is most appropriate for what is to be measured (pencil or long stick to measure the length of the classroom).

subject: Math
cluster: C. Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.

descriptors.cc_approaching: I can count square units in simple figures to find the area, with some guidance (e.g., "With help, I counted squares inside a rectangle to find its area"). I can start to understand that area is measured by counting square units, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can begin to understand that area is the space inside a shape and start counting units, with guidance (e.g., "With help, I know area is like counting the squares inside a shape"). subject: Math

subject: Math
cluster: B. Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.
text: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1-100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1-100 is a multiple of a given one- digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1-100 is prime or composite.
ee_text: Use an understanding of multiplication to show at least one way to determine a product.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use my understanding of factors and multiples to solve real-world problems (e.g., I can figure out how many equal rows of chairs I can make with 36 chairs and 4 chairs in each row). I can explain the difference between prime and composite numbers and give examples of each. I can use my knowledge of factors and multiples to create patterns and relationships between numbers. I can explore more complex number theory concepts, such as finding the greatest common factor or least common multiple of two numbers.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can find all factor pairs for any whole number in the range 1-100 (e.g., I know that the factor pairs of 60 are 1 and 60, 2 and 30, 3 and 20, 4 and 15, 5 and 12, and 6 and 10). I can recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors (e.g., I know that 72 is a multiple of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, and 72). I can consistently determine whether a given whole number in the range 1-100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number (e.g., I know that 99 is not a multiple of 7). I can identify all prime numbers up to 100.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify all the factors of a whole number up to 50 (e.g., I know that the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12). I can recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors (e.g., I know that 12 is a multiple of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12). I can consistently determine whether a given whole number is a multiple of a given one-digit number (e.g., I know that 24 is a multiple of 8). I can identify most prime numbers up to 50.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify some factors of a whole number (e.g., I know that 2 and 4 are factors of 8). I can recognize that a whole number is a multiple of some of its factors (e.g., I know that 8 is a multiple of 2 and 4). I can sometimes determine whether a given whole number is a multiple of a given one-digit number (e.g., I know that 12 is a multiple of 3). I can sometimes identify prime numbers (e.g., I know that 2, 3, and 5 are prime numbers).
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show one way to arrive at a product. I can Using a group of manipulatives, separate into equal groups. I can Provided with counters, pieces of string, or yarn and a work map, make equal sets to arrive at the product. I can when given eight objects that represent the product, make equal sets to represent the factors (e.g., 2 + 2 + 2 + 2) and count to arrive at the product (e.g., 8).
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can make equal groups using numbers within 10 when given manipulatives
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can make equal sets and count to determine the product. I can Using two spinners, spin first spinner to determine the number of groups and the second spinner to determine how many in each group. Supply the numbers from the spinners as factors in the multiplication equation (e.g., x = ).

subject: Math
cluster: C. Generate and analyze patterns.
text: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.
ee_text: Use repeating patterns to make predictions.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule, identify a hidden feature, and apply it to a real-life situation. I can create a pattern of squares where each square has twice the area of the previous square. I notice that the side lengths of the squares increase by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ each time. I can use this pattern to design a set of nesting boxes for birds, where each box is big enough to hold two smaller boxes.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can generate a number pattern that follows a given rule and identify a hidden feature of the pattern. I can start with the number 1 and add 3 to get 4. Then I can add 3 again to get 7. I notice that the numbers are alternating between odd and even. I can explain that this happens because adding 3 to an odd number always gives an even number, and adding 3 to an even number always gives an odd number.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can follow a simple rule to generate a number pattern, but I don't notice any hidden features. I can add 3 to each number in the pattern 1, 4, 7, 10. I can see that the numbers are getting bigger, but I don't notice that they are all even.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can add 3 to a starting number, but I don't understand how to find the next number in the pattern. I can start with the number 1 and add 3 to get 4. But I don't know how to get the next number.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use repeating patterns to make predictions. I can Using a number line, predict what the next number will be when you apply the rule “add 2.” I can Using a shape pattern (e.g., squares, circles, triangles) predict what will come next in the series of three shapes. I can when given a simple ABCABC pattern, indicate, “What comes next?”
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can identify simple patterns I can Student can say the ABAB pattern.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can replicate a pattern and make a prediction. I can Using wooden beads, copy a pattern. Know what should come next. I can Rhythmic or tactile patterns.

subject: Math

descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify the place value of any digit in a two-digit whole number. descriptors.cc_approaching: I can compare fractions with different numerators and denominators by using visual models like fraction strips or number lines. descriptors.ee_approaching: I can identify models of 1/2 and 1/4 in some representations, with assistance.
