subject: Math
cluster: A. Graph points on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
text: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the 0 on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates. Understand that the first number indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of one axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the second axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (e.g., x-axis and x- coordinate, y-axis and y-coordinate).
ee_text: Sort two-dimensional figures and identify the attributes, including number of angles, sides, or corners that they have in common.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use the coordinate plane to represent and solve problems. This includes finding distances between points, plotting shapes, and applying the coordinate plane to real-world situations like reading maps or designing layouts. Example: A student is given a map on a coordinate plane with points representing landmarks. They can calculate the distance between two landmarks, plot a route between multiple points, or even design their own map with specific locations.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can create a coordinate plane with labeled axes and accurately plot points using ordered pairs (x, y). I understand that the first number tells me how far to move along the x-axis, and the second number tells me how far to move along the y-axis. Example: A student can draw a coordinate plane with the x-axis and y-axis labeled, including numbers. If given the ordered pair (3, 5), they can correctly move 3 units to the right from the origin and then 5 units up to plot the point.
descriptors.cc_approaching: Draw two perpendicular lines. Label the lines with numbers, starting from zero on both lines. Place a dot on the lines to represent a point. Use one number to describe the location of the point on one of the lines.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can draw two lines and mark points on them. I am starting to understand that lines and points can be used to show locations. Example: A student can draw two lines on a paper, though they might not be perfectly perpendicular. They can label the lines with some numbers, but they may not start from zero or be in order. They can put dots on the lines to represent locations.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can sort shapes by the number of sides, angles, or corners they have. I can group shapes that share common features, like sorting triangles, squares, and rectangles based on their number of sides or corners.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can look at shapes and show which ones are alike by pointing to features like sides or corners with support. I can identify shapes with similar features, such as all shapes with corners, with help.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can recognize and point to shapes that have the same number of sides or corners with help. I can group shapes by one feature, like the number of sides, with guidance.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Graph points on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
text: Represent real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.
ee_text: Sort two-dimensional figures and identify the attributes, including number of angles, sides, or corners that they have in common.

descriptors.cc_advanced: Students will: Create a coordinate plane to represent a real-world situation, such as the layout of a city park. Plot points on the coordinate plane to represent different locations in the park, such as the playground, the fountain, and the picnic area. Use the coordinate plane to determine the distance between two points in the park. Explain how the concept of graphing points on a coordinate plane can be applied to other areas of study, such as science and social studies.

descriptors.ee_at_target: I can sort shapes by the number of sides, angles, or corners they have. I can group shapes that share common features, like sorting triangles, squares, and rectangles based on their number of sides or corners.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can look at shapes and show which ones are alike by pointing to features like sides or corners with support. I can identify shapes with similar features, such as all shapes with corners, with help.

subject: Math
cluster: B. Classify two-dimensional figures into categories based on their properties.
text: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category. For example, all rectangles have four right angles and squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles.
ee_text: Sort two-dimensional figures and identify the attributes, including number of angles, sides, or corners that they have in common.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use my knowledge about shape categories and their attributes to solve real-world problems and explain my reasoning. Example: A student is challenged to design a tabletop using only quadrilaterals. They can use their knowledge of different quadrilateral types (squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezoids) and their properties to create a functional and aesthetically pleasing design, explaining their choices based on shape attributes.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can explain why shapes within the same category share the same attributes, even if they look different. Example: A student can use a Venn diagram to show the relationship between rectangles and squares. They can explain that all squares belong inside the rectangle circle because they share all rectangle attributes (4 sides, 4 right angles, opposite sides equal), but not all rectangles are squares.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can identify and compare the attributes (sides, angles, etc.) of different two-dimensional shapes, including shapes that belong to the same category. Example: Given a set of quadrilaterals, including squares, rectangles, and trapezoids, a student can sort them by the number of parallel sides. They can identify that some quadrilaterals have two pairs of parallel sides, while others have only one pair, and connect this to the definitions of different quadrilateral types.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify some basic attributes of two-dimensional shapes, like the number of sides or if it has corners. Example: When shown a trapezoid, a student can point out its sides and count that it has four. They can also identify that it has some "straight" sides and some "slanted" sides, demonstrating an early understanding of different side properties.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can sort two-dimensional figures and describe the common attributes such as angles, number of sides, corners (dimension), and color. I can when given shapes, sort by angles and indicate how you sorted them. I can when given shapes sorted based on the number of sides, sort them by another attribute.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can indicate two-dimensional shapes named. I can touch the triangle. I can touch the circle.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can sort figures based on a given attribute. I can sort figures by shape. I can sort figures by size.

subject: Math
cluster: B. Classify two-dimensional figures into categories based on their properties.
text: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.
ee_text: Sort two-dimensional figures and identify the attributes, including number of angles, sides, or corners that they have in common.

descriptors.ee_at_target: I can sort two-dimensional figures and describe the common attributes such as angles, number of sides, corners (dimension), and color. I can when given shapes, sort by angles and indicate how you sorted them. I can when given shapes sorted based on the number of sides, sort them by another attribute.
descriptors.ee_emerging: I can indicate two-dimensional shapes named. I can touch the triangle. I can touch the circle.
descriptors.ee_approaching: I can sort figures based on a given attribute. I can sort figures by shape. I can sort figures by size.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.
text: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities. For example, "The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak." "For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes."
ee_text: Demonstrate a simple ratio relationship.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write ratios for real-world situations in more than one way and explain what each ratio means, including part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use ratio language to describe how two quantities are related. Example: 3 cats and 6 dogs: "For every 1 cat there are 2 dogs," or 3:6.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can write a ratio for a picture or set of objects using a model and sentence frames, such as "For every ___, there are ___."
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can compare two groups of objects and tell which group has more, with pictures and teacher support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show a simple ratio with objects, such as 1 cup for every 2 spoons.

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.
text: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship. For example, "This recipe has a ratio of 3 cups of flour to 4 cups of sugar, so there is 3/4 cup of flour for each cup of sugar." "We paid $75 for 15 hamburgers, which is a rate of $5 per hamburger." Expectations for unit rates in this grade are limited to non-complex fractions.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.7.RP.1.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can find and compare unit rates in real-world problems, like which shop has the better price, and explain my reasoning using rate language.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can find a unit rate a/b from a ratio a:b and describe it with words like "per" and "for each". Example: $75 for 15 burgers is $5 per burger.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find a unit rate with whole numbers when I use a table or picture and a teacher helps me.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can share objects equally into groups and say how many are in each group with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.7.RP.1.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.
text: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number lines, or equations. a. Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios. b. Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed. For example, if it took 7 hours to mow 4 lawns, then at that rate, how many lawns could be mowed in 35 hours? At what rate were lawns being mowed? c. Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 (e.g., 30% of a quantity means 30/100 times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent. d. Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.8.F.1.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can choose a table, tape diagram, double number line or equation to solve multi-step ratio, rate, percent and unit conversion problems, and explain why my method works.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use tables, diagrams and unit rates to solve ratio problems, find a percent of a number, find the whole from a part and percent, and convert units. Example: 30% of 50 = 30/100 × 50 = 15.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can complete a table of equivalent ratios and find a unit rate with simple whole numbers when I have a model or a worked example to follow.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can use objects or pictures to show a ratio, such as 2 red cubes for every 3 blue cubes, with help from my teacher.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.8.F.1.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to divide fractions by fractions.
text: Interpret, represent, and compute division of fractions by fractions and solve word problems by using visual fraction models (e.g., tape diagrams, area models, or number lines), equations, and the relationship between multiplication and division. For example, create a story context for (2/3) ÷ (3/4) such as “How many 3/4 -cup servings are in 2/3 of a cup of yogurt” or “How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length 3/4 mile and area 2/3 square mile?” Explain that (2/3) ÷ (3/4) = 8/9 because 3/4 of 8/9 is 2/3.
ee_text: Compare the relationships between two unit fractions.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write and solve my own word problems that divide a fraction by a fraction, and explain my answer by checking it with multiplication.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can divide fractions by fractions using models and equations, and solve word problems. Example: 2/3 ÷ 3/4 = 8/9 because 3/4 of 8/9 is 2/3.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can divide a fraction by a fraction using a tape diagram or number line with support, for example 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 2.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can use fraction strips to show how many 1/4 pieces fit into 1 whole, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can compare two unit fractions and tell which is bigger, like 1/2 is bigger than 1/4.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Flexibly and efficiently compute with multi-digit numbers and find common factors and multiples.
text: Flexibly and efficiently divide multi-digit whole numbers using strategies or algorithms based on place value, area models, and the properties of operations.
ee_text: Apply the concept of fair share and equal shares to divide.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can divide multi-digit numbers to solve multi-step word problems, explain my strategy, and check my answer using multiplication.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can divide multi-digit whole numbers using place value, area models or the standard algorithm. Example: 1,248 ÷ 24 = 52.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can divide a multi-digit number by a one-digit or two-digit number using an area model or partial quotients with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can share objects into equal groups and use multiplication facts to find how many are in each group.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can share objects fairly into equal groups to divide.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Flexibly and efficiently compute with multi-digit numbers and find common factors and multiples.
text: Flexibly and efficiently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using strategies or algorithms based on place value, visual models, the relationship between operations, and the properties of operations.
ee_text: Use the meaning of multiplication and the properties of operations (e.g., the distributive property) to develop and understand strategies to find products with multiples of 3, 4, and 9 within 100.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve multi-step real-world problems with decimals, such as money or measurement, choose an efficient strategy, and check that my answer is reasonable.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can add, subtract, multiply and divide multi-digit decimals using place value strategies or algorithms. Example: 4.5 x 1.2 = 5.4.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can add and subtract decimals to hundredths and multiply or divide simple decimals using place value charts or models with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can read and write decimals to tenths and line up place values with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use what I know about multiplication and the distributive property to find products of 3, 4 and 9 within 100.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Flexibly and efficiently compute with multi-digit numbers and find common factors and multiples.
text: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1-100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor. For example, express 36 + 8 as 4 (9 + 2).
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use GCF and LCM to solve real-world problems, such as sharing items into equal groups or finding when events repeat, and explain which one I need and why.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can find the GCF of two numbers up to 100 and the LCM of two numbers up to 12, and use the GCF to rewrite a sum. Example: 36 + 8 = 4(9 + 2).
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can list factors or multiples of two small numbers and find a common factor or common multiple when I use a factor list or hundreds chart.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find factor pairs of a small number using arrays or multiplication facts with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.
text: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values (e.g., temperature above/below zero, elevation above/below sea level, credits/debits, positive/negative electric charge); use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of 0 in each situation.
ee_text: Describe quantities having opposite directions or values as positive and negative numbers (e.g., temperature above/below zero).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain how positive and negative numbers describe opposite situations, like money in and money out, and solve a real problem using them.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use positive and negative numbers to show real quantities and explain what 0 means. Example: 10 m below sea level is -10, and 0 is sea level.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can match positive and negative numbers to simple situations, like above or below zero on a thermometer, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can show opposites on a number line, like up and down or above and below zero, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can describe opposite quantities using positive and negative numbers, like temperatures above and below zero.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.
text: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Extend number lines and coordinate axes familiar from previous grades to represent points on the line and in the plane with negative number coordinates. a. Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, e.g., -(-3) = 3, and that 0 is its own opposite. b. Understand signs of numbers in ordered pairs as indicating locations in quadrants of the coordinate plane; recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes. c. Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line; find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane.
ee_text: Describe quantities having opposite directions or values as positive and negative numbers (e.g., temperature above/below zero).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use number lines and the coordinate plane to solve problems with negative numbers and explain how reflecting a point changes the signs of its coordinates.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can place positive and negative numbers on a number line and points in all four quadrants, and find opposites. Example: the opposite of -3 is 3, so -(-3) = 3.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can place integers on a number line and plot points with integer coordinates on a coordinate plane using a model.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can place whole numbers on a number line and plot points in the first quadrant with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use positive and negative numbers to describe opposite amounts, such as temperatures above and below zero.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.
text: Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers. a. Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line. For example, interpret -3 > -7 as a statement that -3 is located to the right of -7 on a number line oriented from left to right. b. Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts. For example, write -3 ℃ > -7 ℃ to express the fact that -3℃ is warmer than -7 ℃. c. Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation. For example, for an account balance of -30 dollars, write |-30| = 30 to describe the size of the debt in dollars. d. Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order. For example, recognize that an account balance less than -30 dollars represents a debt greater than 30 dollars.
ee_text: Describe quantities having opposite directions or values as positive and negative numbers (e.g., temperature above/below zero).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use absolute value and order to solve real-world problems, such as comparing debts or temperatures, and explain why a bigger debt means a smaller balance.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can order rational numbers on a number line, write inequalities in real contexts, and explain absolute value as distance from 0. Example: |-30| = 30.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can order integers on a number line and find the absolute value of an integer with a number line and support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can place positive and negative whole numbers on a number line with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use positive and negative numbers to describe opposite amounts, like temperatures above and below zero.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.
text: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.
ee_text: Describe quantities having opposite directions or values as positive and negative numbers (e.g., temperature above/below zero).

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve real-world problems on a coordinate plane in all four quadrants, such as finding distances on a map, and explain how I used absolute value.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can graph points in all four quadrants and use coordinates and absolute value to find the distance between points that share an x or y coordinate. Example: (2, 3) to (2, -4) is 3 + 4 = 7 units.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can graph points in all four quadrants and count the distance between two points on the same line using the grid.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can plot and name points with whole number coordinates in the first quadrant with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use positive and negative numbers to describe opposite amounts, like temperatures above and below zero.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.
text: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.
ee_text: Evaluate if an equation is true.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write a numerical expression with exponents for a real situation, evaluate it, and explain each step using order of operations.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can write and evaluate numerical expressions with whole-number exponents. Example: 2³ + 4 = 8 + 4 = 12.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the value of a simple power, like 3² = 9, by writing it as repeated multiplication, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can show repeated multiplication with objects or pictures, like 3 groups of 3, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can check if an equation is true, like 3 + 4 = 7.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.
text: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers. a. Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers. For example, express the calculation "Subtract y from 5" as 5 - y. b. Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity. For example, describe the expression 2 (8 + 7) as a product of two factors; view (8 + 7) as both a single entity and a sum of two terms. c. Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole number exponents, in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (order of operations). For example, use the formulas V = s3 and A = 6 s2 to find the volume and surface area of a cube with sides of length s = 1/2.
ee_text: Evaluate if an equation is true.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write and evaluate expressions from real-world formulas, name their parts, and explain why I follow the order of operations.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can write, read and evaluate expressions with variables, name their parts (term, factor, coefficient), and use the order of operations. Example: if s = 2, then 6s² = 6 × 4 = 24.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can evaluate a simple expression by putting a number in for the variable, using the order of operations with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find the value of number expressions with one or two operations, using a step-by-step model.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can check if an equation is true, like 2 + 5 = 7.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.
text: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions. For example, apply the distributive property to the expression 3 (2 + x) to produce the equivalent expression 6 + 3x; apply the distributive property to the expression 24x + 18y to produce the equivalent expression 6 (4x + 3y); apply properties of operations to y + y + y to produce the equivalent expression 3y.
ee_text: Apply the properties of addition to identify equivalent numerical expressions.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can generate equivalent expressions using several properties in one problem and explain why my two expressions are equal.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use the properties of operations, like the distributive property, to write equivalent expressions. Example: 3(2 + x) = 6 + 3x.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can use the distributive property to rewrite simple expressions with whole numbers when I use a model and a teacher helps me.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can show that 3 groups of 2 is the same as 2 + 2 + 2 using objects or pictures.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use the properties of addition to find number expressions that are equal.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.
text: Identify when two expressions are equivalent (e.g., when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them). For example, the expressions y + y + y and 3y are equivalent because they name the same number regardless of which number y stands for.
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can create my own pairs of equivalent expressions and explain, using properties of operations, why they are equal for every value of the variable.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can tell when two expressions are equivalent because they give the same value for any number I substitute. Example: y + y + y and 3y are equivalent.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can substitute a few numbers into two expressions to check if they give the same value, using a table or a model.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can show that two number expressions are equal, such as 3 + 3 + 3 and 3 × 3, using objects or drawings.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Reason about and solve onevariable equations and inequalities.
text: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: Which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.
ee_text: Match an equation to a real-world problem in which variables are used to represent numbers.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can test values from a set in an equation or inequality, find all values that make it true, and explain why the others do not work.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use substitution to decide which numbers from a set make an equation or inequality true. Example: from {2, 3, 4}, x + 5 = 8 is true when x = 3.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can put a given number into a simple equation and check if it is true, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can tell if a number sentence with numbers only, like 4 + 2 = 6, is true or false, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can match an equation with a variable to a real-world problem.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Reason about and solve onevariable equations and inequalities.
text: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.
ee_text: Match an equation to a real-world problem in which variables are used to represent numbers.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write expressions with variables for multi-step real-world problems and explain what the variable stands for.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use a variable to stand for an unknown number and write an expression for a problem. Example: Ali has n pencils and gets 5 more: n + 5.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can choose the correct expression with a variable for a simple word problem from a list.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can use a box or blank to stand for an unknown number in a number sentence, such as 4 + ☐ = 9.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can match an equation to a real-world problem that uses a variable for a number.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Reason about and solve onevariable equations and inequalities.
text: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form x + p = q and px = q for cases in which p, q, and x are all nonnegative rational numbers.
ee_text: Match an equation to a real-world problem in which variables are used to represent numbers.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write and solve equations for multi-step real-world problems with fractions or decimals and explain why my solution makes sense.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can write and solve equations like x + p = q and px = q to solve real-world problems with nonnegative numbers. Example: 4x = 28, so x = 7.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can solve one-step equations with whole numbers using a model or inverse operation with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find the missing number in a simple number sentence, like 5 + ? = 9, using objects.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can match an equation to a real-world problem where a letter stands for a number.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Reason about and solve onevariable equations and inequalities.
text: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write inequalities for real-world limits, show the solutions on a number line, and explain why there are infinitely many solutions.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can write an inequality like x > c or x < c for a real-world condition and show its solutions on a number line. Example: "more than 5 people" is x > 5.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can match a simple situation to an inequality and show it on a number line using an open or closed circle with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can compare two numbers using the symbols > and < with a number line.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Represent and analyze quantitative relationships between dependent and independent variables.
text: Use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another; write an equation to express one quantity, thought of as the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation. For example, in a problem involving motion at constant speed, list and graph ordered pairs of distances and times, and write the equation d = 65t to represent the relationship between distance and time.
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write an equation for two changing quantities in a real problem, use its table and graph to make predictions, and explain how they connect.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can write an equation that shows how a dependent variable changes with an independent variable, and connect it to a table and graph. Example: d = 65t.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can complete a table for a simple rule, like y = 2x, and plot the points, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can continue a simple pattern in a table, like adding 2 each time, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Solve realworld and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.
text: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
ee_text: Solve real-world and mathematical problems about area using unit squares.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can find the area of complex polygons in real-world problems by breaking them into shapes and explain my method.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can find the area of triangles, special quadrilaterals and polygons by splitting them into rectangles and triangles. Example: a triangle with base 8 cm and height 5 cm has area ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the area of a right triangle or rectangle using a formula or grid with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find the area of a rectangle by counting unit squares.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can solve area problems by counting or using unit squares.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Solve realworld and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.
text: Find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths by using physical or virtual unit cubes. Develop (construct) and apply the formulas V = l w h and V = B h to find volumes of right rectangular prisms in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
ee_text: Solve real-world and mathematical problems about volume using unit cubes.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve real-world volume problems with fractional edges, such as filling a box, and explain how V = lwh and V = Bh are connected.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can find the volume of rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths using unit cubes and the formulas V = lwh and V = Bh. Example: 2 x 1/2 x 3 = 3 cubic units.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the volume of rectangular prisms with whole-number edges by counting unit cubes or using V = lwh with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can count cubes to find how many fill a small box with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can solve real-world volume problems by using unit cubes.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Solve realworld and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.
text: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices; use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use coordinates to draw polygons and find side lengths to solve real-world problems, such as finding the perimeter of a garden on a grid.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can draw a polygon on the coordinate plane from its vertices and find the length of sides that share an x or y coordinate. Example: (1, 2) to (5, 2) is 4 units.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can plot given vertices and join them to make a polygon, and count grid units to find the length of a horizontal or vertical side.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can plot points in the first quadrant and connect them in order with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Solve realworld and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.
text: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use nets to find the surface area of 3D figures in real problems, like how much paper wraps a box, and explain my method.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can draw a net of rectangles and triangles for a 3D figure and use it to find surface area. Example: a cube with 2 cm edges has 6 × 4 = 24 cm².
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the area of each face on a given net and add them, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find the area of a rectangle by counting squares, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of statistical variability.
text: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers. For example, "How old am I?" is not a statistical question, but "How old are the students in my school?" is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students' ages.
ee_text: Display data on a graph or table that shows variability in the data.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write my own statistical questions and explain why the answers will vary.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can tell if a question is a statistical question because it expects different answers. Example: "How tall are the students in my class?" is statistical.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can sort questions into "one answer" and "many different answers" with examples and support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can ask a question to my classmates and record their different answers with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show data on a graph or table that shows the answers are different.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of statistical variability.
text: Understand that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape.
ee_text: Display data on a graph or table that shows variability in the data.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare two data distributions by their center, spread and shape and explain what the differences mean in context.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can describe a set of data by its center, its spread and its overall shape. Example: the data clusters around 8 and ranges from 5 to 12.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the center or the spread of a data set shown on a dot plot with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can read a simple graph and say which value happens most often with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show data on a graph or table and point out how the data varies.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Develop understanding of statistical variability.
text: Recognize that a measure of center for a numerical data set summarizes all of its values with a single number, while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare two data sets using a measure of center and a measure of variation and explain what each number tells me about the data.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can explain that a measure of center (like the mean or median) gives one typical value for a data set, and a measure of variation tells how spread out the values are.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find a typical value of a small data set and say whether the values are close together or spread out, using a dot plot.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can order a small set of numbers and find the middle one with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Summarize and describe distributions.
text: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.
ee_text: Display data on a graph or table that shows variability in the data.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can choose the best plot (dot plot, histogram or box plot) for a data set, make it, and explain what it shows.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can display numerical data on a number line using dot plots, histograms and box plots.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can make a dot plot from a small data set on a given number line, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can sort and count data and show it with objects or a tally chart, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can show data on a graph or table that shows how the data varies.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Summarize and describe distributions.
text: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: a. Reporting the number of observations. b. Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement. c. Describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered and the quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation) were given. d. Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.
ee_text: Summarize data distributions shown in graphs or tables.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can summarize a data set, choose the best measures of center and variability for its shape, and explain my choice using the context.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can summarize a data set by giving the number of data points, units, mean or median, a measure of spread, and any unusual values.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the number of data points and the median or mean of a small data set with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can count the data points in a set and find the biggest and smallest values with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can describe what data in a graph or table shows, such as most, least or same.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Analyze proportional relationships and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
text: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas, and other quantities measured in like or different units. For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, compute the unit rate as the complex fraction ½ / ¼ miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour.
ee_text: Use a ratio to model or describe a relationship.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compute unit rates with fractions in multi-step real-world problems and explain which rate is better.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can compute unit rates from ratios of fractions, including different units. Example: 1/2 mile in 1/4 hour is 2 miles per hour.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find unit rates when the numbers are whole numbers or simple fractions, using a table or diagram with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find how much for one item using whole numbers and objects with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use a ratio to model or describe a relationship.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Analyze proportional relationships and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
text: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities. a. Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin. b. Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships. c. Represent proportional relationships by equations. For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn. d. Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.
ee_text: Use a ratio to model or describe a relationship.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can decide if real-world relationships are proportional, write equations like y = kx, and explain what points such as (0, 0) and (1, r) mean in the situation.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can test if a relationship is proportional using a table or graph, find the constant of proportionality, and write an equation. Example: $3 per item means t = 3n.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can use a table of equivalent ratios to find the unit rate and tell if the graph is a straight line through (0, 0) with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can complete a simple ratio table, such as 1 box has 4 pens, 2 boxes have 8 pens, using objects or pictures.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use a ratio to describe or model a relationship.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Analyze proportional relationships and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
text: Use proportional relationships to solve multi-step ratio and percent problems. Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.
ee_text: Use a ratio to model or describe a relationship.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve multi-step percent problems, like a discount followed by tax, and explain each step and why my answer makes sense.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use proportional relationships to solve multi-step ratio and percent problems, like tax, tips and percent increase. Example: 20% off a 50 QAR shirt costs 40 QAR.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find a simple percent of a number, like 10% or 50%, using a model or table, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can use a ratio table or picture to show a simple ratio, like 2 red for every 3 blue, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use a ratio to show or describe a relationship, like 2 cups of water for every 1 cup of rice.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers.
text: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line. a. Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0. For example, if you earn $10 and then spend $10, you are left with $0. b. Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. c. Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts. d. Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.
ee_text: Add fractions with like denominators (halves, thirds, fourths, and tenths) with sums less than or equal to one.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can add and subtract rational numbers in multi-step real-world problems and explain my answers using a number line and absolute value.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can add and subtract positive and negative numbers, using a number line and the rule p - q = p + (-q). Example: -5 - 3 = -5 + (-3) = -8.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can add and subtract integers using a number line or counters with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can add and subtract whole numbers on a number line and show that a number plus its opposite makes 0 with counters.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can add fractions with the same denominator (halves, thirds, fourths, tenths) when the total is 1 or less.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers.
text: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers. a. Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (-1)(-1) = 1 and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. b. Understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero, and every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If p and q are integers, then -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q). Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts. c. Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers. d. Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.
ee_text: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication, division, and fractions. a. Multiply within 100 using strategies such as the properties of operations [e.g., knowing that 7 x 6 can be thought of as 7 groups of 6 so one could think 5 groups of 6 is 30 and 2 more groups of 6 is 12 and 30 + 12 = 42 (informal use of the distributive property)]. b. Solve division problems within 100, including divisors of 1-5 and 10, without remainders. c-d. Express a fraction with a denominator of 10 as a decimal.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can multiply and divide rational numbers in real-world problems, explain the sign rules, and decide if a decimal repeats or terminates.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can multiply and divide positive and negative rational numbers, use the sign rules, and change fractions to decimals using long division. Example: (-3)(-4) = 12.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can multiply and divide integers using sign rules on a chart and change simple fractions to decimals with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can multiply and divide whole numbers within 100 with models.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can multiply within 100 using strategies, divide within 100 by 1 to 5 or 10, and write fractions with a denominator of 10 as decimals.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers.
text: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers. (Note: Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions.)
ee_text: Using real world examples, compare quantities represented as decimals to tenths.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve multi-step real-world problems with positive and negative fractions and decimals and explain whether my answer makes sense.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can add, subtract, multiply and divide rational numbers to solve real-world and math problems. Example: The temperature is -3°C and drops 4.5°C, so it is -7.5°C.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can solve one-step problems with integers or simple fractions and decimals using a number line or a model.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can add and subtract whole numbers and simple fractions in word problems with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can compare decimal amounts to tenths in real-world examples.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
text: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.
ee_text: Use the properties of operations as strategies to demonstrate that expressions are equivalent.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can add, subtract, factor and expand linear expressions with fractions or decimals, and explain which property I used at each step.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use properties of operations to add, subtract, factor and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients. Example: 2(x + 3) - x = x + 6.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can combine like terms and expand simple expressions with whole numbers, like 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can use the distributive property with numbers, like 3 × (4 + 2) = 3 × 4 + 3 × 2, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use properties of operations to show that two expressions are equivalent.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
text: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related. For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that "increase by 5%" is the same as "multiply by 1.05."
ee_text: Identify an arithmetic sequence of whole numbers with a whole number common difference.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can rewrite an expression in a real-world problem in a different form and explain what the new form tells me about the problem.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can rewrite an expression in a different form to show how the quantities are related. Example: a + 0.05a = 1.05a, so a 5% increase is the same as multiplying by 1.05.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can tell when two simple expressions are equivalent using a model, such as x + x + x = 3x.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can combine like objects or numbers to show the same amount in two ways, such as 2 + 2 + 2 = 3 × 2.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can identify a number pattern that adds the same whole number each time, such as 3, 6, 9, 12.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations.
text: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies. For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50.
ee_text: Not applicable.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve multi-step real-world problems with positive and negative numbers in any form and explain how I checked my answer with estimation.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can solve multi-step problems with rational numbers, convert between fractions, decimals and percents, and check with estimation. Example: a 10% raise on $25 is $2.50, so $27.50.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can solve two-step problems with whole numbers or simple decimals and estimate my answer with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can solve one-step word problems with whole numbers using a model or drawing.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations.
text: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. a. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Flexibly and efficiently apply the properties of operations and equality to solve equations of these forms. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? b. Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make and describe the solutions.
ee_text: Use the concept of equality to solve one-step addition and subtraction equations with models.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can write and solve equations and inequalities for real-world problems, compare an algebraic and an arithmetic solution, and explain what my answer means.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can solve word problems with equations like px + q = r or p(x + q) = r and inequalities like px + q > r, and graph the solution. Example: 2w + 12 = 54, so w = 21.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can solve two-step equations with whole numbers using a model or a step-by-step guide.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can solve one-step equations like x + 5 = 12 using objects, a balance model or a bar model.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can use models to solve one-step addition and subtraction equations by keeping both sides equal.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them.
text: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale.
ee_text: Match two similar geometric shapes that are proportional in size and have the same orientation.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use a scale drawing to solve real problems with lengths and areas, and redraw it at a new scale, explaining my reasoning.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use a scale drawing to find actual lengths and areas, and redraw it at a different scale. Example: if 1 cm = 2 m, then 5 cm = 10 m.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can use a simple scale to find one actual length, like 1 cm = 10 m, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can tell which of two shapes is bigger or smaller and by how many times, using grid paper, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can match two similar shapes that have the same shape and position but different sizes.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them.
text: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
ee_text: Recognize geometric shapes with given conditions.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can explain why some side or angle measures make one triangle, many triangles, or no triangle.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can draw triangles from given side lengths or angle measures and tell if the conditions make one triangle, more than one, or none.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can draw a triangle with given measures using a ruler and protractor with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name and draw triangles and other basic shapes, and measure a side with a ruler.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can recognize shapes that match given conditions, such as a triangle with a right angle.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them.
text: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three dimensional figures parallel to the base, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.
ee_text: Match a two-dimensional shape with a three-dimensional shape that shares an attribute.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can predict and explain the shapes made by slicing prisms and pyramids, and compare slices taken at different heights.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can describe the 2D shape made when I slice a right rectangular prism or pyramid parallel to its base. Example: a slice of a square pyramid is a square.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can name the 2D shape of a slice when I see a model or picture of the cut with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can name the faces of a 3D shape using real objects with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can match a 2D shape with a 3D shape that shares an attribute.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Solve real-life and mathematical problems involving angle measure, area, surface area, and volume.
text: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle.
ee_text: Determine the perimeter of a rectangle.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use the circle formulas to solve multi-step real-world problems and explain how the area and circumference of a circle are related.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use C = πd (or 2πr) and A = πr² to find the circumference and area of a circle. Example: r = 3 cm, A ≈ 3.14 × 9 = 28.26 cm².
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the circumference or area of a circle when I am given the formula and the radius or diameter.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find the radius and diameter of a circle and measure them with a ruler with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can find the perimeter of a rectangle.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Solve real-life and mathematical problems involving angle measure, area, surface area, and volume.
text: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.
ee_text: Recognize angles that are acute, obtuse, and right.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use angle facts in multi-step problems to write and solve equations for unknown angles, and explain my reasoning.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use supplementary, complementary, vertical and adjacent angles to write and solve equations for an unknown angle. Example: x + 40 = 90, so x = 50°.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find a missing angle when two angles make a straight line (180°) or a right angle (90°), with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can identify right angles and angles on a straight line in a picture, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can recognize acute, obtuse and right angles.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Solve real-life and mathematical problems involving angle measure, area, surface area, and volume.
text: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume, and surface area of two-and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.
ee_text: Determine the area of a rectangle using the formula for length x width and confirm the result using tiling or partitioning into unit squares.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can solve multi-step real-world problems with area, volume and surface area of composite shapes and explain my strategy.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can solve problems about area, volume and surface area of 2D and 3D objects made of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes and right prisms. Example: a box 2 × 3 × 4 cm has volume 24 cm³.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the area of rectangles and triangles and the volume of rectangular prisms using formulas with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can find area by counting unit squares and volume by counting unit cubes.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can find the area of a rectangle using length × width and check it by counting unit squares.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Use random sampling to draw inferences about population.
text: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.
ee_text: Answer a data related question, given a model of the data from a student experiment or collection.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can design a random sampling plan for a real question and explain why my sample is representative and my inference is valid.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can explain that random samples tend to represent a population and use sample data to make inferences about that population.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can tell if a sample is random or not random with support and examples.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can answer a question about a group using a small set of data with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can answer a question about data using a model of data from a class experiment or collection.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: A. Use random sampling to draw inferences about population.
text: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions. For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.
ee_text: Answer a data related question, given a model of the data from a student experiment or collection.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can take several random samples, compare their results, and explain how far off my estimate or prediction about the population might be.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use data from a random sample to make an estimate or prediction about a population. Example: 12 of 30 students chose red, so about 40% of the school might choose red.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can use a sample to make a simple prediction about a group when I am given the data and sentence frames.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can read a simple table or bar graph of survey results and say which choice was most popular with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can answer a question about data from an experiment or collection using a model of the data.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
text: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability. For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, about twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.
ee_text: Compare two sets of data found within a single data display such as a picture graph, line plot, or bar graph.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare two data sets by how much they overlap, describe the difference in centers as a multiple of variability, and explain what it means.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can compare two data distributions with similar spread by finding the difference between their centers as a multiple of a measure of variability.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can compare the means of two dot plots and say which is greater and by how much, with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can look at two dot plots and say which group has bigger values, with help.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can compare two sets of data in one picture graph, line plot or bar graph.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: B. Draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
text: Use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations. For example, decide whether the words in a chapter of a seventh-grade science book are generally longer than the words in a chapter of a fourth-grade science book.
ee_text: Not applicable. See M.EE.SP.ID.4.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can use center and spread to compare two groups of data and explain if the difference is meaningful.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use the mean, median, range or mean absolute deviation to compare two groups of data and make an informal conclusion.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can find the median or mean of two data sets and say which is greater with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can compare two small data sets on a graph and say which has bigger values with support.
descriptors.ee_at_target: Not applicable. See M.EE.SP.ID.4.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.
text: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.
ee_text: Describe the probability of events occurring as possible or impossible.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can compare the probabilities of events in real situations and explain my choices using numbers from 0 to 1.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can describe probability as a number from 0 to 1 and tell if an event is unlikely, equally likely or likely. Example: 1/2 means equally likely.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can place events on a probability line from impossible to certain with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can sort events as possible or impossible using pictures.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can describe whether an event is possible or impossible.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.
text: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability. For example, when rolling a number cube 600 times, predict that a 3 or 6 would be rolled roughly 200 times, but probably not exactly 200 times.
ee_text: Describe the probability of events occurring as possible or impossible.

descriptors.cc_advanced: I can run an experiment, compare the results to the expected probability, and explain why the results are close to, but not exactly, what I predicted.
descriptors.cc_at_target: I can use data from repeated trials to estimate a probability and predict how often an outcome will happen. Example: Roll a cube 600 times, a 3 or 6 should come up about 200 times.
descriptors.cc_approaching: I can collect data from a simple experiment, like flipping a coin, and say about how often an outcome happened with support.
descriptors.cc_emerging: I can say whether an event is likely or unlikely using simple chance activities.
descriptors.ee_at_target: I can describe whether an event is possible or impossible.

source: Wisconsin Standards for Mathematics (2021); Wisconsin Essential Elements for Mathematics (2022)

subject: Math
cluster: C. Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.
text: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy. a. Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events. For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected. b. Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process. For example, find the approximate probability that a spinning penny will land heads up or that a tossed paper cup will land open-end down. Do the outcomes for the spinning penny appear to be equally likely based on the observed frequencies
ee_text: Describe the probability of events occurring as possible or impossible.
